lines.text: Perhaps he was thinking of the thousands who were being attacked and killed on
the roads and railways as they tried to reach their homeland. There was much in
those days of violence to sadden Jinnah who was a man of very strong feelings
ichough he rarely showed it. Yet those who were close to him on Independence
Day sometimes saw for a few moments a happier man. Once he went to the
balcony of the Governor House, from where he could see without being seen, and
as he looked on the crowd still cheering in the streets outside, he smiled. In that
smile could be seen the warm hearted man behind the stern Quaid-e-Azam.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah was at this time tired and far from well but he had the
satisfaction of knowing that the greater
part of his work was done. By the force of
his determination and leadership,a people
who had once been a defeated group, with
little to hope for, in an empire ruled by a
foreign power, had become the greatest of
the Muslim States and the 5th largest
nation in the world.Seventy million
people, who once had no country to call
their own, had become a nation -- with
great ideals and a great faith. A few days
after he landed in Karachi, Muhammad Ali
